sm: The host of CrossPolitic reflects on the November 3rd elections, in which Texas Democrats flipped the governor's office, the Senate seat, lieutenant governor, attorney general and the state House. He mainly blames Governor Greg Abbott, saying he repeatedly promised to lower property taxes without doing so, and contrasts him with Ron DeSantis, who grew his support in Florida. He argues Republicans with majorities get little done while Democrats pass big legislation, and says conservatives should lead boldly, as Charlie Kirk did. He ends by saying Christians should be neither too heavenly minded nor carnally minded.

The host continues, saying Christians should be spiritually minded and engaged, like Christ healing the leper. He cites consultant Joseph Backholm's claim that if eighty percent of Seattle's churchgoers voted, the city council would be Christianized, and says the evangelical vote dropped to seventeen percent. He argues the church's apathy is the real problem. He then introduces Texas state representative Brent Money, who was just reelected. Money agrees largely with the Abbott thesis but says the Trump effect also mattered. He says a fourth term is a bad idea, supports term limits for the governor and lieutenant governor, and begins discussing Ken Paxton.

Brent Money says Ken Paxton was an excellent attorney general but carries personal baggage, including a publicly known affair, that hurt him with independents. He says Abbott and Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick had been in office too long and pushed a movie industry subsidy, a state-funded Alzheimer's research program, and a THC crackdown that hurt veterans. He adds that importing Argentinian beef angered Texas ranchers. He says Republican wins have mostly been stopping the left, while affordability has been neglected. The host agrees, saying property tax cuts are conservatism 101, and that he favors term limits only for weak governors.

Money says the Florida model was what Texas should have followed, and that Republican primary voters kept Abbott in 2022. He says Abbott's third term was his best, but it was too late, and he blames a Washington effect, since Congress never codified Trump's border and spending cuts or passed the SAVE Act. He says Texas's budget grew about four percent per capita each year over twelve years, versus two percent in Florida. The host says the old guard avoids real conservative reform, mentions twenty-five thousand churches in Texas, and says Republicans in power descend into infighting and excuses.

The host says Abbott and other statewide leaders deserve the blame and will simply retire without accountability. Money notes Texas has won a business-friendly state award thirteen years in a row, yet wages, traffic, crime and property taxes have worsened. He says about eighteen percent of Texans were born abroad, that Indian-American voters went around eighty percent Democratic, and that Republicans should have closed the border and stopped rewarding foreign labor. They discuss the Democrats gaining about two million votes while Abbott's total stayed flat. Money calls for election integrity but warns against scapegoating fraud alone.

Money says he believes Texas can come back, calling the result a rejection of Washington and Austin rather than of conservative ideas, as shown by bond measures failing. He expects two to four years of gridlock, with Republicans holding the Senate eighteen to ten and Democrats the House. He says Republicans must offer a positive message, not just attack Democrats, noting Brandon Gill and James Talarico both won the same district by double digits. The host describes his own Latah County in Idaho, where demographic change favors conservatives. Money calls for better candidates and a stronger message.

Money says most people ignore politics until election time, so Republicans need year-round discipling, large families and teaching of political philosophy. He says Democrats won on ground organization while Republicans relied on ads, mailers and texts, and that conservatives need door knocking all the time. On the next presidential race, he says he is no national pundit but expects JD Vance, Ron DeSantis, Glenn Youngkin, Ted Cruz and perhaps Tom Cotton to run. He does not think Marco Rubio will run against Vance. The host closes by urging Christians to care about politics without anxiety and to focus on family, home and neighborhood.
